To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the gills of the Blue Crab (Callinectes sapides) are the site of the greatest metabolic activity in the crab, and that this activity can be measured in terms of oxygen consumption and ATP content; 2) that the gill tissues of the Blue Crab are capable of responding to osmotic stress by adjusting their metabolism, and that this metabolic adjustment can be quantified in terms of oxygen uptake and ATP content.
the gills of the crab Callinectes are osmoconformers that have the capability to maintain a constant internal ionic environment by adjusting their rate of respiration.
respiration rate of excised gill tissue from blue crabs was directly dependent on salinity and size of the gills, and inversely dependent on ATP content of the tissue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the energetics of the blue crab Callinectes sp. in relation to osmotic stress.
the effects of osmotic stress on the energy metabolism of crab gill tissues and the role of the gill in the overall osmoregulatory process of the blue crab.
the effects of salinity on respiration rate and ATP concentration of the gill tissues of the blue crab.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the gills of the crab, Callinects sapidus, are capable of maintaining their normal metabolic rates and ATP concentrations over a range of salinities, and that the energy source for this process is ATP.
the gills of the crab are a major site for the production of ATP and that this ATP is used for cellular accommodation.
ATP is the source of energy for osmoregulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the gills of the crab have a high metabolic rate and that this rate is maintained in response to salinity changes.
the gill is a major site of energy utilization for osmoregulation in the blue crab.

the gill tissue of the blue crab is capable of responding to osmotic stress in a manner that would be expected to maintain the ionic composition of the cytoplasmic fluid at a level that would be compatible with normal physiological functioning of the tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the blue crab, like other marine invertebrates, has evolved to be able to tolerate a wide range of salinity.

when the gills of a blue crab are subjected to an osmotic stress (e.g., a change in the external salinity), the process of cellular adjustment is an energetic one and that the ultimate energy source for this process is ATP.
ATP is required for the process of cellular adaptation to osmotic stress.
